title: Assisted suicide threatens the dignity and safety of Black communities in Maryland
summary: Black Marylanders already get inequitable treatment across virtually every metric of health care, writes Paul Sullins, and policymakers considering assisted suicide should know that it will only risk magnifying those disparities.
content:
by Paul Sullins, Maryland Matters December 24, 2025

by Paul Sullins, Maryland Matters December 24, 2025

Maryland lawmakers may again consider legalizing physician-assisted suicide (PAS) this session. Before they do, they should confront an uncomfortable truth: In a state where African Americans already face stark inequalities in health care, PAS, even if intended compassionately, would introduce the power of state-authorized death into a system that has long failed to protect Black Marylanders’ health, dignity and, too often, their lives.

The Maryland Department of Health documents clear and persistent inequalities in health outcomes in this state. Black residents are more likely to die of cancer even though they are less likely than whites to develop it. Black infants die at more than double the rate of white infants. Black mothers die in pregnancy at twice the rate of white mothers. And the proportion of Black physicians in the state is far lower than their share of the population. What happens when we add the power of prescribing death to a health care system that already does not treat all lives equally?

This concern is the subject of my new Maryland Family Institute Research Brief, “Knee on the Neck: Assisted Suicide and the African-American Experience in Maryland.” The title reflects the sober reality: For Black Marylanders, PAS risks magnifying the ultimate outcome under the guise of impartial health care.

African Americans have good reason to be cautious about giving physicians greater authority over life-and-death decisions. Georgetown scholars Patricia King and Leslie Wolf have observed that Black patients “have been abused, neglected and exploited” within American medicine and therefore “have reason to believe that their lives are not valued in the same way as whites.”

That historical memory is not distant. It echoes today in biased diagnostic patterns, under-treated pain and survival gaps across multiple diseases.

PAS does not correct these injustices. It amplifies them.

In states that have legalized PAS, very few physicians are willing to participate.Oregon, the first state to adopt the practice, has roughly 13,000 physicians, yet in a recent year, only 146 wrote any lethal prescriptions. Just 32 doctors wrote most of them, and one doctor wrote 51. When life-ending authority is so concentrated, the biases of a tiny number of persons will dominate its practice. Maryland would be naive to assume that racial prejudice, whether conscious or unconscious, would play no role in determining which patients are encouraged toward death.

PAS can be especially harmful in Black communities, where churches and pastors play a central role in affirming that every life, even in suffering, has God-given worth and dignity. For many African Americans who have spent a lifetime resisting messages of inferiority, a physician’s authoritative suggestion of suicide can easily, if unintentionally, displace the preaching of hope and faith with a darker message: Your life is more burdensome than valuable. Your death may be the more reasonable path.

Maryland need not guess how this plays out. Three decades ago, after extensive review, a bipartisan New York task force unanimously rejected PAS, warning it would be “profoundly  dangerous” for stigmatized populations and impossible to regulate equitably. Maryland’s racial disparities today are no better than New York’s were then. If PAS posed “extraordinary risks” there, it poses equal if not greater risks here.

I write as a sociologist, a married Catholic priest, a father in an interracial family and a lifelong Marylander, formerly living in South Baltimore and now Prince George’s County. We must not adopt a policy that makes premature death the most accessible “treatment option” for those already receiving unequal care. PAS will not bring justice, equality or dignity. It will bring quiet but devastating pressure on those whose lives our health care system already struggles to protect.
